title: Decision-making 101
primary_topics: The simplified Aristotelian syllogism framework for judicial decision-making: L x F = D (law times facts equals decision)
Why most cases are won or lost on factual issues rather than legal ones -- and why trial court fact-finding is authoritative
How legal complications (jurisdiction, bail, novel crimes, appeals) delay and complicate criminal prosecutions beyond the simple syllogism
sub_topics: Aristotelian syllogism: major (legal) premise x minor (factual) premise = logical conclusion; example: homicide charge
Nine years of tertiary study to become a lawyer -- yet law conclusively presumes everyone knows the law; ignorance is no excuse; truth is not a valid defense (jaywalking example)
Most litigations won or lost on factual issues (minor premise), not legal ones
Facts proven only in RTC or municipal courts -- not CA or SC which does not examine witnesses
SC relies on trial court fact-finding because trial judges have firsthand impressions (People v. Delavin, Feb. 27, 1987)
Witness credibility indicators from People v. Rivera (Oct. 1, 1993): timidity, forthrightness, surliness, belligerence, indignation, embarrassment, hesitancy, glibness, evasiveness, insolence
Trial judges: lowest in hierarchy but indispensable; virtual kings in acquittals (immediately executory, cannot be appealed -- double jeopardy)
Double jeopardy: No person shall be put twice in jeopardy of punishment for the same offense
Legal complications: jurisdiction (GMA charged in RTC but Sandiganbayan has jurisdiction), bail, preliminary investigation, novel crime constitutionality (plunder)
Post-judgment complications: self-defense claims, homicide vs murder, improper penalty
signature_phrases: judicial decision-making can be reduced to an Aristotelian syllogism
law times facts equals decision, or L x F = D
Ignorance of the law is never an excuse for violating it
truth is not a valid defense!
The trial judge had the opportunity to observe the witnesses personally
Timidity, forthrightness, surliness, belligerence, indignation, embarrassment, hesitancy, glibness, evasiveness, insolence
Trial judges are virtual kings and almost irreversible when they acquit
a judgment of acquittal is immediately executory and cannot be appealed
All these questions of law could interminably complicate and delay a criminal prosecution

cases: People v. Delavin (Feb. 27, 1987) -- trial court fact-finding authority
People v. Rivera (Oct. 1, 1993) -- witness credibility indicators
events: GMA charged in RTC (jurisdiction challenge illustration)

stances.claim: Judicial decision-making follows L x F = D, but most cases turn not on the legal premise but on the factual premise -- whether the accused committed the act -- making trial court fact-finding the critical and most contested battleground.

Trial courts are the indispensable foundation of the judicial system because they are the only courts that can determine facts firsthand -- making their factual findings authoritative on appeal and their acquittals absolutely final (double jeopardy).
stances.rhetorical_move: trial-court-primacy argument (lowest in hierarchy but indispensable and often irreversible)

stances.claim: Legal complications -- jurisdiction challenges, bail petitions, novel-crime constitutionality questions, and post-conviction appeals -- can delay criminal prosecutions interminably.

notable_anecdotes: The jaywalking example for ignorance-of-law: if caught jaywalking, you cannot be acquitted because you did not know it was prohibited -- here, truth is not a valid defense! -- the most accessible illustration of the conclusive presumption of legal knowledge.

People v. Rivera (1993) witness credibility vocabulary -- timidity, forthrightness, surliness, belligerence, indignation, embarrassment, hesitancy, glibness, evasiveness, insolence -- preserved verbatim as the most vivid judicial vocabulary list in any CJ column.

The GMA jurisdiction example: charged in RTC but counsel challenges because the Sandiganbayan has jurisdiction over high officials even after their terms -- a preliminary legal issue that can delay a trial for years before it begins.
target_audience: Law students and incoming bar examinees seeking a foundational overview
Non-lawyers following high-profile criminal cases who want to understand why trials take so long
Civic readers following the GMA Sandiganbayan case
Judges and practitioners reflecting on fundamental principles

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban introduces judicial decision-making through the Aristotelian syllogism framework: law times facts equals decision (L x F = D). He illustrates with a homicide example (major premise: anyone who kills shall be jailed; minor premise: Pedro killed Juan; conclusion: Pedro shall be jailed) and notes that despite nine years of tertiary study required to become a lawyer, ignorance of the law is never an excuse -- 'truth is not a valid defense' against jaywalking, for instance. Most litigations are won or lost not on legal issues but on the factual minor premise -- whether the act was committed. Facts are proven only in trial courts, not in the CA or SC, which rely on the trial court's fact-finding authority because the trial judge has firsthand impressions of witnesses' demeanor, tone, and credibility (quoting People v. Delavin, 1987, and People v. Rivera, 1993 -- the latter listing 'timidity, forthrightness, surliness, belligerence, indignation, embarrassment, hesitancy, glibness, evasiveness, insolence' as credibility indicators). Though lowest in the judicial hierarchy, trial judges are 'virtual kings' in acquittals -- which are immediately executory and cannot be appealed under the double jeopardy prohibition. He then shows how legal complications -- jurisdiction challenges (e.g., GMA charged in RTC when the Sandiganbayan has jurisdiction over high officials), bail petitions, preliminary investigation disputes, novel-crime constitutionality questions (e.g., plunder), and post-judgment appeals on crime classification or penalty -- can delay criminal prosecutions interminably, preventing the simple syllogism from producing a timely result.
